title: Does a university education help you earn more?
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou questions the assumption behind the UK graduate premium debate, that going to university causes higher earnings. She argues that even nuanced critiques, such as publishing earnings by subject and institution, assume the premium is caused by university rather than selection, and compares it to a Rolex premium: people who wear Rolexes earn more, but nobody concludes that buying one raises income. She sets out the human capital versus signalling debate, noting the policy stakes: if signalling dominates, vast public and private sums are wasted. Because many well-paid jobs are restricted to graduates, causal research is complex and inconclusive, which is striking given how embedded human capital theory is. She argues that standardised assessment of learning would be a better measure of university quality than earnings, and proposes compulsory national assessment modules in degrees. The post links assessment, evidence and what education actually adds to the learner.
points: The graduate premium shows a correlation between degrees and earnings, not proof that university teaches valuable skills.
The human capital view says degrees impart skills while the signalling view says they mainly certify prior attainment to employers.
If signalling dominates, degrees could largely be replaced by a basic test at 18, saving enormous sums.
Earnings data is a poor measure of university value because it misses learning for its own sake, undervalues vital low-paid jobs and reflects regional pay.
Compulsory standardised assessment in degrees would give direct evidence of what universities teach, as schools already have.
quotes: But graduate income data does not prove this causal chain. Yes, it is true that people who go to university earn more, on average, than people who don’t.

The signalling side says that the graduate premium is caused by the signal that is sent by a degree. Universities select their students based on prior attainment. Employers use degrees as a cheap (for them!) way to select employees who are already smart.

If it turns out the returns to a degree are mostly due to signalling, then we are wasting gigantic sums of private and public money. We could essentially replace degrees with some kind of basic test taken at age 18 and that would provide employers with what they are currently getting with hugely expensive three-year degree courses.
But of course, that won’t work, because lots of jobs are restricted to graduates. Maybe the non-grads would have done perfectly well at them, but they never get a chance.

As a result, a lot of the research in this area is hugely complex and ultimately quite inconclusive. That in itself is quite striking though – given how embedded the human capital theory is, and how much it governs the public debate and policymaking in this area, you would expect there to be some quite solid evidence in its favour!
Earnings data doesn’t capture the value of learning for its own sake. It undervalues low-paid but socially vital jobs.

Given the scale of public subsidy and private debt involved, why not make some form of standardised assessment compulsory for all degrees? This could take a variety of different formats: maybe certain subjects all have to have a couple of shared “national” exam modules covering the content that every university will teach.
